text:
283. How is it possible for a child to immediately doubt what instruction provides? Such doubt would signify only that the child lacked the capacity to acquire certain language-activities.

284. From earliest times, human beings have killed animals, exploiting their fur and bones and other constituents for various purposes. Throughout this history, they have counted on finding similar anatomical structures in any similar creature. Their learning has been experiential. We can see from their conduct that they hold certain things to be definitively so, whether they articulate this conviction or remain silent. This observation is not prescriptive—I am not claiming that human beings should conduct themselves in this manner. I am claiming only that they do conduct themselves in this manner.

285. If someone searches for something, perhaps digging through a particular location, his behavior demonstrates that he believes what he seeks to be there.

286. What we believe is a function of what we learn. All of us believe that reaching the moon is impossible. But there might exist people who believe it possible and believe it sometimes occurs. We say: these people lack much knowledge that we possess. However certain they may be of their conviction, they are mistaken and we know this.

When we compare our knowledge-system with theirs, theirs is evidently far inferior.

287. The squirrel does not employ inductive inference to conclude that it will require stored provisions next winter as well. We likewise require no law of induction to justify our conduct or our predictions.

288. I know—not merely that the earth existed long before my birth, but also that it is massive, that this has been established, that I and the rest of humanity have ancestors, that books exist concerning all this, that such books do not falsify, and so forth. Do I know all this? I believe it. This knowledge-corpus has been transmitted to me, and I possess no grounds for doubting it; on the contrary, I possess abundant confirmation.

Why should I not say that I know all this? Is that not what one does say?

But not only do I know, or believe, all that—others do as well. More precisely, I believe that they believe it.

289. I am firmly convinced that others believe, believe they know, that all that is in fact the case.

290. I myself wrote in my book that children learn to understand a word in such and such a manner. Do I know that, or do I believe it? Why in such a case do I write not "I believe etc." but simply the indicative sentence?

291. We know that the earth is round. We have definitively ascertained its roundness.

We shall maintain this view, unless our entire way of regarding nature changes. "How do you know that?"—I believe it.

292. Subsequent experiments cannot falsify our earlier ones. At most they may alter our entire way of regarding things.

293. The same applies to the sentence "water boils at 100°C."

294. This is how we acquire conviction. This is what is called "being rightly convinced."

295. In this sense, does one not possess a proof of the proposition? But that the same occurrence has repeated itself is not a proof of it, though we do say that it gives us justification to assume it.

296. This is what we call an "empirical foundation" for our assumptions.

297. For we learn not merely that such and such experiments yielded those and those results, but also the conclusion that is drawn from them. There is nothing objectionable in our doing so. The inferred proposition functions as an instrument for a definite use.

298. "We are quite sure of it" does not mean merely that every individual person is certain of it. It means that we belong to a community bound together by science and education.

299. We are satisfied that the earth is round.

300. Not all revisions of our views occupy the same level.

301. Suppose it were not true that the earth had already existed long before I was born—how should we imagine the error being discovered?

302. It serves no purpose to say "Perhaps we are mistaken" when, if no evidence is trustworthy, trust is excluded in the case of the present evidence.

303. If, for example, we have always been miscalculating, and twelve times twelve is not one hundred and forty-four, why should we trust any other calculation? Of course, that formulation is mistaken.

304. But I am not making an error about twelve times twelve being one hundred and forty-four. I may say later that I was confused just then, but not that I was making an error.

305. Here once more what is needed is a step analogous to the one taken in relativity theory.

306. "I don't know if this is a hand." But do you know what the word "hand" means? Do not respond "I know what it means now for me." And is it not an empirical fact—that this word is used in this way?

307. What is remarkable here is that when I am completely certain of how the words are used, harbor no doubt about it, I can still provide no grounds for my way of proceeding. If I attempted to do so, I could supply a thousand grounds, but none as certain as the very thing they were supposed to ground.

308. "Knowledge" and "certainty" belong to different categories. They are not two mental states comparable to, say, "surmising" and "being sure." (Here I assume that it is meaningful for me to say "I know what (for example) the word 'doubt' means" and that this sentence indicates that the word "doubt" has a logical role.) What interests us now is not being sure but knowledge. That is, we are interested in the fact that concerning certain empirical propositions no doubt can exist if judgment-making is to be possible at all. Alternatively: I am inclined to believe that not everything possessing the form of an empirical proposition is one.

309. Is it that rule and empirical proposition merge into one another?

310. One says "I know" where one can also say "I believe" or "I suspect"; where one can find out. (If I say "I know that he is in pain" it would be possible—though unusual—to add: "but of course I may be wrong.") But not "I know that 12 × 12 = 144"; here "I may be wrong" makes no sense.

Of course, when propositions of natural science are in question, what is experimentally established today could be overthrown tomorrow by further experiments. But this is different with propositions that form the foundation of all our operating with thoughts (with language).

311. If "I know etc." is conceived as a grammatical proposition, naturally the "I" cannot be important. It means "There is no such thing as a doubt in this case" or "The expression 'I do not know' makes no sense in this case." One must inquire what follows from this for the propositions which logic considers.

312. Once more: it comes down to this: "I know" expresses comfortable certainty, not the certainty that is still struggling.

313. Now I would like to regard this certainty as something that lies beyond being justified or unjustified; as something animal, so to speak.

314. How does someone judge which is his right and which his left hand? How do I know that my judgment will agree with someone else's? How do I know that this color is blue? If I don't trust myself here, why should I trust anyone else's judgment? Is there a why? Must I not begin to trust somewhere? That is to say: somewhere I must begin with not-doubting; and that is not, so to speak, hasty but excusable: it is part of judging.

315. In this way I might define: I call a proposition "empirical" if people could acquire it through experience—if experience can convince them of it. This distinguishes grammatical propositions from empirical ones.

316. What we call "testing" a proposition stands in a particular logical relationship to the proposition. (If a liquid is called "the solvent" of such-and-such a substance, obviously there must be a way of establishing whether it dissolves the substance.)

317. The proposition "I am in pain" is tested by my groaning—but the proposition "2 × 2 = 4" is not tested by counting.
